steps.intro: “In”, “like” and “to” are single letters fixed to the front of a word, just like “the”. Listen for b-, k- and l-.

cards.title: Three one-letter prepositions
body: בְּ means in, at, with or by. כְּ means like or as. לְ means to or for (and often “of”, as in the psalm titles: לְדָוִד, “of David”).

They take a shewa, בְּ כְּ לְ, but it changes when the next word makes it awkward: before another shewa it becomes i (בִּמְקוֹם, in a place), and before a hateph vowel it borrows that vowel (לַעֲשׂוֹת, to do).

examples.en: in a place: shewa before shewa becomes i

cards.title: With “the”: the ה drops out
body: When one of these comes before “the”, the article's ה disappears and the preposition takes its vowel. בְּ + הַמִּדְבָּר is בַּמִּדְבָּר, “in the wilderness”.
So בַּ, כַּ or לַ with a dot after, or בָּ, כָּ, לָ, means the preposition and “the” together.

cards.title: מִן, from, and the separate prepositions
body: מִן, from, can stand alone (often joined with ־) or be fixed to the front as מִ with a doubled next letter: מִמִּצְרַיִם. Before a throat letter, which can't be doubled, it is מֵ: מֵהָעִיר.
Other prepositions are ordinary words: אֶל to, עַל on or over, עִם with, עַד as far as or until, תַּחַת under, אַחַר after.

cards.explain: לְ (to) has taken the article's patah, and the dot in מּ is the article's doubling: to the king.
בַּ with a dot after it: בְּ (in) plus “the”.

cards.prompt: Match each preposition to its meaning.

cards.explain: בָּאָרֶץ, in the land: בְּ has taken the article's vowel (qamets, because א can't be doubled).

cards.prompt: Make “from Egypt”: מִ fixed to the front of מִּצְרַיִם.
cards.explain: מִן shortens to מִ and doubles the next letter: מִמִּצְרַיִם.

cards.prompt: Why is it מֵהָעִיר (from the city), not מִהָּעִיר?
options: ה is a throat letter and can't be doubled
cards.explain: מִן doubles the next letter, but ה can't be doubled, so the vowel lengthens to מֵ.

steps.intro: Find each preposition fixed to the front of a word.

cards.note: לָאוֹר (to the light) and וְלַחֹשֶׁךְ (and to the darkness): לְ with “the”. “God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.”
מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם, “from the land of Egypt”, and מִבֵּית עֲבָדִים, “from the house of slaves”: “from” fixed to the front twice.
